name: AT42QT1010-MAHR
title: AT42QT1010: one-key capacitive touch and proximity sensor IC with digital output
summary: A single-channel capacitive sensor chip that turns one electrode into a touch key or a proximity sensor and drives a push-pull output high while it detects. It measures by bursts of charge-transfer cycles into one external sample capacitor, calibrates itself, tracks drift, filters noise and spreads its oscillator frequency. A mode pin picks fast response, low power (about 34 µA at 3 V) or synchronisation to an external signal. It runs from 1.8 to 5.5 V and comes in a SOT23-6 or a 2 × 2 mm UDFN/USON-8.

circuits.title: Basic circuit, SOT23-6
circuits.description: The chip runs from VDD with VSS to ground. Cs sits between the two sense pins SNSK and SNS; SNSK also feeds the sense electrode through the series resistor Rs, which keeps ESD and EMC energy off the pin. Cx is the electrode's own capacitance to ground, which a finger raises. OUT goes high while a touch is detected. SYNC/MODE sets the run mode: high for Fast, low for Low Power, a changing signal for SYNC. A 100 nF ceramic bypass capacitor sits tight across VDD and VSS.

circuits.title: HeartBeat pulses with a pull-up resistor (SOT23-6)
circuits.description: A resistor Ro from VDD to OUT turns each 15 µs three-state gap of the output into a short positive pulse while no touch is detected, which a counter, flip-flop or one-shot can watch to confirm the chip is alive. During a detection OUT is already high and the pulses do not show.
notes: SNSK, SNS and SYNC/MODE are wired as in the basic circuit.

circuits.title: HeartBeat pulses in either output state, with a microcontroller (SOT23-6)
circuits.description: One microcontroller port drives OUT's load resistor Ro and a second port reads OUT directly. The controller switches the load resistor to VSS or VDD according to the output's present state, so the HeartBeat gap shows as a pulse in both states.
notes: Supply, sense pins and SYNC/MODE are wired as in the basic circuit.

operation.text: The chip measures the key with bursts of charge-transfer cycles: each cycle charges the electrode and moves its charge onto Cs, and the count needed is the signal. Working in bursts keeps the average current in microamps, lowers RF emission and susceptibility, and still answers quickly. All switches and the measuring hardware are inside the chip. A touch has to be seen on four bursts in a row before OUT goes high.

The electrode connects to SNSK only. Cs must be much larger than Cx: Cx is typically 5 to 20 pF, Cs about 2 to 50 nF. Stray capacitance on either sense pin lowers gain, so the sense traces are kept short and thin and away from power, ground and copper pour. Every trace and part on SNS and SNSK is itself touch sensitive. A series resistor Rs between SNSK and the electrode suppresses ESD and EMC effects.

Sensitivity depends on Cs, electrode size, shape and orientation, the object sensed, the panel's thickness and material, and how well sensor and object couple to ground. It rises with a larger electrode, a thinner panel, a panel of higher dielectric constant, or a larger Cs; a larger Cs costs response time and current. Electrode area brings little once the electrode is much bigger than the finger, and too much Cx cuts gain. Ground or metal near the electrode or beneath it, or along its SNSK trace, loads Cx and lowers gain, so ground is kept clear of them. A smaller Cs lowers sensitivity.

Raised sensitivity lets the part detect a nearby hand rather than a touch. A very large electrode and a larger Cs are used; the slower response this brings matters little when the target is a large object.
With SYNC/MODE held high the part bursts continuously, about 1 ms apart, for the quickest response and the highest current.

With SYNC/MODE held low the part sleeps about 80 ms after each burst. When a burst suggests a touch it switches to Fast mode until the detect integrator confirms or rejects the touch, then goes back to sleeping between bursts.

A waveform on SYNC/MODE synchronises the bursts, to keep several QT1010s from interfering with each other or to reject low-frequency noise such as 50 Hz or 60 Hz mains. SYNC/MODE is read as each burst ends: high keeps Fast mode, low sends the part to sleep and into SYNC mode, so the low part of the sync signal must last longer than a burst. In SYNC mode the part sleeps after each burst and wakes for a new burst on each edge of SYNC; with a train of short pulses (over 10 µs) it bursts on each falling edge only. If SYNC stays still for longer than the LP sleep period (about 80 ms) the part returns to Fast or LP mode according to the pin's level. SYNC mode has no detect integrator, so each detection counts, and the Max On-duration and recalibration timeout scale with the sync period, the timeout being counted in measurements.
A detection is a signal change of 10 counts from the reference level, which itself follows drift slowly. Hysteresis is 2 counts of the reference-to-threshold difference.

If a detection lasts longer than a timer allows, as when something rests on the key, the part fully recalibrates and OUT goes low. The timer runs from the burst rate and is about 60 s at 3 V in LP mode; it changes a little with Cs and greatly with the sync spacing in SYNC mode, falling to about 6 s at 3 V with a 60 Hz sync.

A counter steps up on each burst that shows a detection and resets to zero on any burst that does not; OUT goes high when it reaches four. This rejects noise and brief brushes. In LP mode the part runs fast while counting, then returns to LP operation by itself.

There is no recalibration pin. The part calibrates at power-up and after the recalibration timeout. Because its current is small, the chip can be powered from a logic gate or microcontroller port, and cycling that supply forces a recalibration; most CMOS outputs have low enough source resistance for this.

While nothing is detected the reference level is slowly pulled toward the raw signal, its rate slew-limited, with the threshold and hysteresis tied to it; during a detection it stops. Compensation is faster for a falling signal than a rising one, so an approaching finger is not tracked away, yet the removal of an object that had been compensated for is recovered from within a few seconds. Large Cs with small Cx makes compensation look slower.

Response time follows the run mode and the burst length, and burst length follows Cs and Cx: more Cs slows the response, more Cx speeds it. LP and SYNC modes respond much more slowly than Fast mode because the bursts are further apart.
The internal oscillator is swept by ±7.5% during each burst, spreading emitted noise across a band and lowering susceptibility, since there is no single burst frequency.

OUT goes high on a detection and stays high until the detection ends or the Max On-duration runs out, whichever comes first. After a timeout the part recalibrates and OUT is low until a new detection.

In every mode OUT is switched to three-state for 15 µs once before each burst. A pull-up on OUT turns this into a positive pulse that shows only while no touch is detected; a microcontroller can move the load resistor to VSS or VDD to see the pulse in both states. Relays usually ignore the pulse and its duty cycle is too low to show on an LED. An RC filter on OUT removes it; a high-impedance CMOS input needs nothing, or at most a small capacitor between OUT and VSS.

OUT sinks or sources up to 2 mA. With Cs above 20 nF the OUT current is kept under 1 mA, because load current drops voltage on the die and bond wires and can shift the signal enough to make detection unstable.

Cs sets sensitivity. Thicker panels and lower dielectric constant need larger values; the usual range is 2 to 50 nF, and larger values call for a more stable dielectric. Cs should be of a stable dielectric, X7R ceramic or PPS film, with 5 % tolerance for consistent units; PPS is preferred where high sensitivity means long bursts. For battery operation a higher value is recommended, typically 8.2 nF.
The underside centre pad connects to ground. No tracks other than ground run under the body.

At 3 V the average current in Fast mode is under 500 µA. Gradual Vdd changes are tracked, but rapid steps, spikes and sags upset it, so a supply shared with digital circuits must be clean; a regulator dedicated to the QT1010 is strongly recommended. An LDO can be used, though many have poor line and load transient response.

Place the chip so the SNSK trace is short, which cuts both stray Cx and low-frequency pickup. Cs and Rs go right at the chip so the trace from Rs to SNSK is very short and picks up little high-frequency noise. A ground plane may sit under the chip and its parts, but the trace from Rs to the electrode, and the electrode, stay clear of ground, other signals and power, beside and beneath. All-SMT construction gives the best EMC.
A 100 nF ceramic capacitor directly across VDD and VSS, very close to both pins, is required to prevent latch-up under large Vdd transients such as an ESD event.
After first power-up the part takes about 100 ms to start, and OUT is not valid in that time. The supply must rise at 10 V/s or faster for a proper start.
